content: Hydroxypropyl cellulose is a cellulose derivative approved by the FDA for treating moderate to severe dry eye syndromes, including keratoconjunctivitis sicca. It is particularly indicated for patients who remain symptomatic after adequate trials of artificial tear solutions. It is also used in conditions such as exposure keratitis, decreased corneal sensitivity, and recurrent corneal erosions. The typical dosage involves inserting one hydroxypropyl cellulose ophthalmic insert into each eye once daily. Some patients may require twice-daily use for optimal results. Clinical experience suggests that several weeks of use may be necessary before achieving satisfactory symptom improvement. The insert is placed in the inferior cul-de-sac of the eye, beneath the base of the tarsus, avoiding direct contact with the cornea or the eyelid at the tarsal plate level. Improper placement may result in the insert being expelled into the interpalpebral fissure, causing foreign body sensations. Patients should practice insertion and removal under the supervision of a licensed practitioner until proficient. Common adverse reactions include transient blurred vision, ocular discomfort or irritation, matting or stickiness of eyelashes, photophobia, hypersensitivity, eyelid edema, and hyperemia. If symptoms worsen, patients should inspect the conjunctival sac to ensure proper placement of the insert. If symptoms persist, the insert should be removed, and the patient should contact their healthcare provider. Hydroxypropyl cellulose is contraindicated in patients with hypersensitivity to the substance. Patients should be cautioned against rubbing their eyes, especially upon waking, to prevent dislodging the insert. If transient blurred vision occurs, the insert may be removed a few hours after insertion, and a new one can be placed if needed. There is limited information regarding off-label uses, pediatric safety and efficacy, and specific populations such as pregnant or nursing women, geriatric patients, or those with renal or hepatic impairment. Hydroxypropyl cellulose is physiologically inert and not metabolized, as demonstrated in animal studies. It dissolves completely within 14 to 18 hours after placement in the conjunctival sac. The product is supplied as sterile, translucent, rod-shaped inserts, each containing 5 mg of hydroxypropyl cellulose, with no preservatives or additional ingredients. It is packaged with illustrated instructions and a special applicator for insertion. Storage should be below 30°C (86°F). Hydroxypropyl cellulose stabilizes and thickens the precorneal tear film, prolonging tear film breakup time and providing lubrication and protection to the eye. It reduces symptoms such as conjunctival hyperemia, corneal and conjunctival staining, exudation, itching, burning, foreign body sensation, photophobia, dryness, and blurred vision. Studies have shown that it is more effective and preferred by patients compared to artificial tears, with improvements observed in symptoms associated with keratoconjunctivitis sicca over long-term use.
